claim: Adaptive immune responses are triggered by antigenic peptides presented on major histocompatibility complex class I (MHC I) at the surface of pathogen-infected or cancerous cells.
source: Adaptive immune responses are triggered by antigenic peptides presented on major histocompatibility complex class I (MHC I) at the surface of pathogen-infected or cancerous cells.
evidence: This is supported by established scientific knowledge about the adaptive immune system and MHC I function.

claim: Formation of stable peptide-MHC I complexes is facilitated by tapasin and TAPBPR.
source: Formation of stable peptide-MHC I complexes is facilitated by tapasin and TAPBPR, two related MHC I-specific chaperones that catalyze selective loading of suitable peptides onto MHC I in a process called peptide editing or proofreading.
evidence: This is supported by established scientific knowledge and citations in the manuscript.

claim: Tapasin and TAPBPR are MHC I-specific chaperones that catalyze selective loading of suitable peptides onto MHC I in a process called peptide editing or proofreading.
source: Formation of stable peptide-MHC I complexes is facilitated by tapasin and TAPBPR, two related MHC I-specific chaperones that catalyze selective loading of suitable peptides onto MHC I in a process called peptide editing or proofreading.
evidence: This is supported by established scientific knowledge and citations in the manuscript.

claim: MHC I complexes must pass a quality control step performed by UGGT1 on their journey to the cell surface.
source: On their journey to the cell surface, MHC I complexes must pass a quality control step performed by UGGT1, which senses the folding status of the transiting N-linked glycoproteins in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER).
evidence: This is supported by established scientific knowledge about ER quality control.

claim: UGGT1 senses the folding status of transiting N-linked glycoproteins in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER).
source: On their journey to the cell surface, MHC I complexes must pass a quality control step performed by UGGT1, which senses the folding status of the transiting N-linked glycoproteins in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER).
evidence: This is supported by established scientific knowledge about UGGT1 function.

claim: UGGT1 reglucosylates non-native glycoproteins and thereby allows them to revisit the ER folding machinery.
source: UGGT1 reglucosylates non-native glycoproteins and thereby allows them to revisit the ER folding machinery.
evidence: This is supported by established scientific knowledge about UGGT1 function in the calnexin/calreticulin cycle.

claim: TAPBPR promotes reglucosylation of peptide-free MHC I by UGGT1.
source: By combining glycoengineering with liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry, we show that TAPBPR promotes reglucosylation of peptide-free MHC I by UGGT1.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the in-vitro reglucosylation assay using LC-MS analysis.

claim: UGGT1 cooperates with TAPBPR in fulfilling a crucial function in the quality control mechanisms of antigen processing and presentation.
source: Thus, UGGT1 cooperates with TAPBPR in fulfilling a crucial function in the quality control mechanisms of antigen processing and presentation.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing TAPBPR-mediated reglucosylation of MHC I by UGGT1.

claim: Peptidic ligands of pMHC I complexes are primarily derived from proteasomal degradation products of cytosolic proteins.
source: The peptidic ligands of these peptide-MHC I (pMHC I) complexes are primarily derived from proteasomal degradation products of cytosolic proteins and are transported into the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) by the ATP-binding cassette (ABC) transporter associated with antigen processing (TAP1/2) (Thomas and Tampé, 2020; Thomas and Tampé, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Peptides are transported into the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) by the ATP-binding cassette (ABC) transporter associated with antigen processing (TAP1/2).
source: The peptidic ligands of these peptide-MHC I (pMHC I) complexes are primarily derived from proteasomal degradation products of cytosolic proteins and are transported into the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) by the ATP-binding cassette (ABC) transporter associated with antigen processing (TAP1/2) (Thomas and Tampé, 2020; Thomas and Tampé, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Inside the ER, peptides can be further trimmed by aminopeptidases, in particular ERAP1/2, generating ligands of optimal length for fitting in the MHC I binding groove.
source: Inside the ER, peptides can be further trimmed by aminopeptidases, in particular ERAP1/2, generating ligands of optimal length for fitting in the MHC I binding groove (Hammer et al., 2007; Hattori and Tsujimoto, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The antigen transporter TAP1/2 is the central component of a dynamic supramolecular machinery called the peptide-loading complex (PLC).
source: The antigen transporter TAP1/2 is the central component of a dynamic supramolecular machinery called the peptide-loading complex (PLC) coordinating peptide transfer across the ER membrane with peptide loading onto MHC I inside the ER lumen (Blees et al., 2017; Trowitzsch and Tampé, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The peptide-loading complex (PLC) coordinates peptide transfer across the ER membrane with peptide loading onto MHC I inside the ER lumen.
source: The antigen transporter TAP1/2 is the central component of a dynamic supramolecular machinery called the peptide-loading complex (PLC) coordinating peptide transfer across the ER membrane with peptide loading onto MHC I inside the ER lumen (Blees et al., 2017; Trowitzsch and Tampé, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Tapasin and TAPBPR stabilize intrinsically unstable peptide-deficient MHC I.
source: Both Tsn and TAPBPR stabilize intrinsically unstable peptide-deficient MHC I and act as peptide editors or proofreaders by accelerating peptide exchange and selecting high-affinity peptide ligands (Boyle et al., 2013; Chen and Bouvier, 2007; Fleischmann et al., 2015; Hermann et al., 2013; Hermann et al., 2015; Morozov et al., 2016; Sagert et al., 2020; Tan et al., 2002; Wearsch and Cresswell, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Tapasin and TAPBPR act as peptide editors or proofreaders by accelerating peptide exchange and selecting high-affinity peptide ligands.
source: Both Tsn and TAPBPR stabilize intrinsically unstable peptide-deficient MHC I and act as peptide editors or proofreaders by accelerating peptide exchange and selecting high-affinity peptide ligands (Boyle et al., 2013; Chen and Bouvier, 2007; Fleischmann et al., 2015; Hermann et al., 2013; Hermann et al., 2015; Morozov et al., 2016; Sagert et al., 2020; Tan et al., 2002; Wearsch and Cresswell, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The affinity optimization of MHC I-associated peptides is crucial for immunosurveillance by T lymphocytes, priming of naive T cells, and T cell differentiation.
source: The affinity optimization of MHC I-associated peptides is crucial for immunosurveillance by T lymphocytes, priming of naive T cells, and T cell differentiation.
evidence: This is supported by established scientific knowledge about T cell biology.

claim: The catalytic principles of peptide optimization have been revealed by crystal structures of the TAPBPR-MHC I complex.
source: The catalytic principles of peptide optimization have been revealed by crystal structures of the TAPBPR-MHC I complex (Jiang et al., 2017; Thomas and Tampé, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous structural studies.

claim: Insights into the interaction characteristics between Tsn and peptide-receptive MHC I have been gained by structures of Tsn-ERp57-H2-Db and Tsn-HLA-B*44:05.
source: Insights into the interaction characteristics between Tsn and peptide-receptive MHC I have been gained by structures of Tsn-ERp57-H2-Db (Müller et al., 2022) and Tsn-HLA-B*44:05 (Jiang et al., 2022), respectively.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous structural studies.

claim: Tapasin is a key constituent of the PLC.
source: While Tsn is a key constituent of the PLC, TAPBPR functions outside the PLC and downstream of Tsn in the secretory pathway, even beyond the ER in the Golgi compartment (Boyle et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: TAPBPR functions outside the PLC and downstream of Tsn in the secretory pathway, even beyond the ER in the Golgi compartment.
source: While Tsn is a key constituent of the PLC, TAPBPR functions outside the PLC and downstream of Tsn in the secretory pathway, even beyond the ER in the Golgi compartment (Boyle et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: MHC I complexes are glycoproteins consisting of a highly polymorphic, N-glycosylated heavy chain and the invariant light chain β2-microglobulin (β2m).
source: As glycoproteins consisting of a highly polymorphic, N-glycosylated heavy chain and the invariant light chain β2-microglobulin (β2m), MHC I complexes are also subject to quality control by the calnexin/calreticulin cycle in which the major glycoprotein folding sensor UDP-glucose:glycoprotein glucosyltransferase 1 (UGGT1) fulfills a crucial role (Wearsch et al., 2011; Zhang et al., 2011)
evidence: This is supported by established scientific knowledge about MHC I structure.

claim: MHC I complexes are subject to quality control by the calnexin/calreticulin cycle in which UGGT1 fulfills a crucial role.
source: As glycoproteins consisting of a highly polymorphic, N-glycosylated heavy chain and the invariant light chain β2-microglobulin (β2m), MHC I complexes are also subject to quality control by the calnexin/calreticulin cycle in which the major glycoprotein folding sensor UDP-glucose:glycoprotein glucosyltransferase 1 (UGGT1) fulfills a crucial role (Wearsch et al., 2011; Zhang et al., 2011)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The two outermost glucose residues of the core N-glycan Glc3Man9GlcNAc2 are sequentially cleaved off by α-glucosidase I and II (GluI/II).
source: The two outermost glucose residues of the core N-glycan Glc3Man9GlcNAc2, which is co-translationally transferred to a conserved asparagine of the nascent MHC I heavy chain, are sequentially cleaved off by α-glucosidase I and II (GluI/II), and the resulting mono-glucosylated dodecasaccharide (Glc1Man9GlcNAc2) is specifically recognized by the scaffolding lectin-like ER chaperones calnexin and calreticulin.
evidence: This is supported by established scientific knowledge about N-glycan processing.

claim: The core N-glycan Glc3Man9GlcNAc2 is co-translationally transferred to a conserved asparagine of the nascent MHC I heavy chain.
source: The two outermost glucose residues of the core N-glycan Glc3Man9GlcNAc2, which is co-translationally transferred to a conserved asparagine of the nascent MHC I heavy chain, are sequentially cleaved off by α-glucosidase I and II (GluI/II), and the resulting mono-glucosylated dodecasaccharide (Glc1Man9GlcNAc2) is specifically recognized by the scaffolding lectin-like ER chaperones calnexin and calreticulin.
evidence: This is supported by established scientific knowledge about N-glycosylation.

claim: The mono-glucosylated dodecasaccharide (Glc1Man9GlcNAc2) is specifically recognized by the scaffolding lectin-like ER chaperones calnexin and calreticulin.
source: The two outermost glucose residues of the core N-glycan Glc3Man9GlcNAc2, which is co-translationally transferred to a conserved asparagine of the nascent MHC I heavy chain, are sequentially cleaved off by α-glucosidase I and II (GluI/II), and the resulting mono-glucosylated dodecasaccharide (Glc1Man9GlcNAc2) is specifically recognized by the scaffolding lectin-like ER chaperones calnexin and calreticulin.
evidence: This is supported by established scientific knowledge about the calnexin/calreticulin cycle.

claim: Calreticulin escorts MHC I to the PLC for peptide loading.
source: The latter escorts MHC I to the PLC for peptide loading.
evidence: This is supported by established scientific knowledge about calreticulin function.

claim: GluII can cleave off the terminal glucose once pMHC I complexes are no longer protected by calreticulin.
source: Once pMHC I complexes are no longer protected by calreticulin, GluII can cleave off the terminal glucose (Domnick et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: pMHC I complexes that have acquired optimal peptides via the PLC or in a PLC-independent fashion and have adopted their native fold when their last glucose residue is removed can exit the ER and travel via the Golgi apparatus to the cell surface.
source: Those pMHC I complexes that have acquired optimal peptides via the PLC or in a PLC-independent fashion and have adopted their native fold when their last glucose residue is removed, can exit the ER and travel via the Golgi apparatus to the cell surface where they are scanned by T cell receptors (TCRs) on cytotoxic T cells and natural killer (NK) cell receptors.
evidence: This is supported by established scientific knowledge about MHC I trafficking.

claim: pMHC I complexes at the cell surface are scanned by T cell receptors (TCRs) on cytotoxic T cells and natural killer (NK) cell receptors.
source: Those pMHC I complexes that have acquired optimal peptides via the PLC or in a PLC-independent fashion and have adopted their native fold when their last glucose residue is removed, can exit the ER and travel via the Golgi apparatus to the cell surface where they are scanned by T cell receptors (TCRs) on cytotoxic T cells and natural killer (NK) cell receptors.
evidence: This is supported by established scientific knowledge about immune surveillance.

claim: The Man9GlcNAc2 glycan of MHC I complexes that are suboptimally loaded or empty and partially misfolded is recognized and reglucosylated by UGGT1.
source: However, the Man9GlcNAc2 glycan of MHC I complexes that are suboptimally loaded or empty and partially misfolded is recognized and reglucosylated by UGGT1, allowing the newly formed mono-glucosylated MHC I species to be re-engaged by calnexin or calreticulin and given another chance to acquire a suitable peptide, for example, by revisiting the PLC (Wearsch et al., 2011; Zhang et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Reglucosylation by UGGT1 allows the newly formed mono-glucosylated MHC I species to be re-engaged by calnexin or calreticulin and given another chance to acquire a suitable peptide.
source: However, the Man9GlcNAc2 glycan of MHC I complexes that are suboptimally loaded or empty and partially misfolded is recognized and reglucosylated by UGGT1, allowing the newly formed mono-glucosylated MHC I species to be re-engaged by calnexin or calreticulin and given another chance to acquire a suitable peptide, for example, by revisiting the PLC (Wearsch et al., 2011; Zhang et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The UGGT1-mediated quality control of MHC I has been shown to be directly promoted by the peptide editor TAPBPR, based on immunoprecipitation experiments from cell lysates and mass spectrometry.
source: Most interestingly, the UGGT1-mediated quality control of MHC I has recently been shown to be directly promoted by the peptide editor TAPBPR, based on a combination of immunoprecipitation experiments from cell lysates and mass spectrometry (Neerincx et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: HLA-A*68:02 is a favored client of TAPBPR.
source: HLA-A*68:02 is a favored client of TAPBPR (Boyle et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Kifunensine is an α-mannosidase I inhibitor that arrests glycan processing primarily at the Man9GlcNAc2 stage.
source: Kifunensine is an α-mannosidase I inhibitor that arrests glycan processing primarily at the Man9GlcNAc2 stage (Chang et al., 2007; Elbein, 1991).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The highest yield of Man9GlcNAc2 was achieved with 10 µM kifunensine.
source: The highest yield of Man9GlcNAc2 was achieved with 10 µM kifunensine, while increasing the concentration to 20 µM did not improve the yield (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Increasing kifunensine concentration to 20 µM did not improve the yield of Man9GlcNAc2.
source: The highest yield of Man9GlcNAc2 was achieved with 10 µM kifunensine, while increasing the concentration to 20 µM did not improve the yield (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: After Strep-Tactin affinity purification and TEV protease cleavage, the peptide-receptive HLA-A*68:02-TAPBPR complex eluted as monodisperse sample at the expected size of 90 kDa during size-exclusion chromatography (SEC).
source: After Strep-Tactin affinity purification and Tobacco etch virus (TEV) protease cleavage, the peptide-receptive HLA-A*68:02-TAPBPR complex eluted as monodisperse sample at the expected size of 90 kDa during size-exclusion chromatography (SEC) (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Sep15 has been shown to enhance UGGT1 activity.
source: His-tagged human UGGT1 was co-expressed and secreted from insect cells with its binding partner Sep15 (15 kDa selenoprotein), which has been shown to enhance UGGT1 activity (Takeda et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Small amounts of a degradation product at ~37 kDa representing the C-terminal catalytic glucosyltransferase domain were detected in addition to full-length UGGT1.
source: In addition to full-length UGGT1, we detected small amounts of a degradation product at ~37 kDa by SDS-PAGE and immunoblotting, representing the C-terminal catalytic glucosyltransferase domain, in line with previous observations (Guerin and Parodi, 2003; Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A, and citations to previous work.

claim: UGGT1 exhibited clear UDP-glucose-dependent glucosyltransferase activity towards Man9GlcNAc2-HLA-A*68:02-TAPBPR.
source: UGGT1 exhibited clear UDP-glucose-dependent glucosyltransferase activity towards Man9GlcNAc2-HLA-A*68:02-TAPBPR, as judged by the appearance of the peak corresponding to the HLA-A*68:02-linked mono-glucosylated Glc1Man9GlcNAc2 glycan species in the mass spectra (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A–C.

claim: The D1316N mutant of UGGT1 was inactive.
source: The D1316N mutant of UGGT1, in which the first aspartate of the Ca2+-coordinating DxD motif in the catalytic site (Roversi et al., 2017) is mutated, was inactive (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D and citations to previous work.

claim: Activity of mutant UGGT1D1316N could not be restored by adding 5 µM purified Sep15.
source: Activity of mutant UGGT1D1316N could not be restored by adding 5 µM purified Sep15 (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: UGGT1-catalyzed reglucosylation reactions reached saturation at ~80% product formation.
source: Interestingly, UGGT1-catalyzed reglucosylation reactions in general reached saturation at ~80% product formation (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Saturation of UGGT1-catalyzed reglucosylation could not be overcome by raising the temperature.
source: This saturation could be overcome neither by raising the temperature (Figure 2F) nor by increasing the enzyme concentration (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Saturation of UGGT1-catalyzed reglucosylation could not be overcome by increasing the enzyme concentration.
source: This saturation could be overcome neither by raising the temperature (Figure 2F) nor by increasing the enzyme concentration (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Binding of high-affinity peptide leads to TAPBPR dissociation.
source: Binding of high-affinity peptide leads to TAPBPR dissociation, allowing the peptide-loaded Man9GlcNAc2-HLA-A*68:02 to be isolated by size-exclusion chromatography (SEC; Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: The peptide-deficient state of the MHC I was generated by photo-cleavage of the bound peptide and dissociation of the resulting low-affinity peptide fragments.
source: The peptide-deficient state of the MHC I was generated by photo-cleavage of the bound peptide and dissociation of the resulting low-affinity peptide fragments.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental design described in the manuscript.

claim: The peptide-loading status of pMHC I and empty MHC I was confirmed by LC-MS.
source: The peptide-loading status of pMHC I and empty MHC I was confirmed by LC-MS (Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The generated peptide-free Man9GlcNAc2-HLA-A*68:02 was shown to bind the conformation-specific antibody W6/32, demonstrating that the peptide-receptive MHC I remain stable throughout the experiment.
source: Additionally, the generated peptide-free Man9GlcNAc2-HLA-A*68:02 was shown to bind the conformation-specific antibody W6/32, demonstrating that the peptide-receptive MHC I remain stable throughout the experiment (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Neither the peptide-loaded nor the peptide-deficient HLA-A*68:02 were reglucosylated by UGGT1 in the absence of TAPBPR.
source: Most strikingly, neither the peptide-loaded nor the peptide-deficient HLA-A*68:02 were reglucosylated by UGGT1 in the absence of TAPBPR (Figure 3D–F), but we were able to restore UGGT1 activity towards peptide-deficient HLA-A*68:02 by adding TAPBPR (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D–F.

claim: UGGT1 activity towards peptide-deficient HLA-A*68:02 was restored by adding TAPBPR.
source: Most strikingly, neither the peptide-loaded nor the peptide-deficient HLA-A*68:02 were reglucosylated by UGGT1 in the absence of TAPBPR (Figure 3D–F), but we were able to restore UGGT1 activity towards peptide-deficient HLA-A*68:02 by adding TAPBPR (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Loading of a low-affinity (suboptimal) peptide onto the peptide-receptive MHC I could not restore the susceptibility of UGGT1.
source: Moreover, loading of a low-affinity (suboptimal) peptide onto the peptide-receptive MHC I could not restore the susceptibility of UGGT1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 3), further emphasizing the critical role of TAPBPR.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: TAPBPR is an essential mediator in the UGGT1-catalyzed reglucosylation of the human MHC I allomorph HLA-A*68:02.
source: These results demonstrate that the MHC I-specific chaperone TAPBPR is an essential mediator in the UGGT1-catalyzed reglucosylation of the human MHC I allomorph HLA-A*68:02.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing that TAPBPR is necessary and sufficient for UGGT1-mediated reglucosylation of HLA-A*68:02.

claim: The ER-lumenal part of TAPBPR consists of an N-terminal composite domain composed of coalesced seven-stranded β barrel and immunoglobulin (Ig)-like (V type) folds, and a C-terminal IgC1 domain.
source: The ER-lumenal part of the peptide proofreader TAPBPR consists of an N-terminal composite domain composed of coalesced seven-stranded β barrel and immunoglobulin (Ig)-like (V type) folds, and a C-terminal IgC1 domain (Jiang et al., 2017; Thomas and Tampé, 2017; Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous structural studies and Figure 4A.

claim: TAPBPR contacts the peptide-receptive MHC I client through a large concave surface of its N-terminal composite domain, which interacts mainly with the α2–1-helix region of the MHC I.
source: TAPBPR contacts the peptide-receptive MHC I client through a large concave surface of its N-terminal composite domain, which interacts mainly with the α2–1-helix region of the MHC I, and via interfaces of its C-terminal IgC1 domain with β2m and the α3 domain of the MHC I heavy chain (Jiang et al., 2017; Thomas and Tampé, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous structural studies.

claim: TAPBPR contacts the peptide-receptive MHC I client via interfaces of its C-terminal IgC1 domain with β2m and the α3 domain of the MHC I heavy chain.
source: TAPBPR contacts the peptide-receptive MHC I client through a large concave surface of its N-terminal composite domain, which interacts mainly with the α2–1-helix region of the MHC I, and via interfaces of its C-terminal IgC1 domain with β2m and the α3 domain of the MHC I heavy chain (Jiang et al., 2017; Thomas and Tampé, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous structural studies.

claim: Of the seven cysteines in the ER-lumenal portion of TAPBPR, four are involved in two disulfide bridges in the N-terminal domain, and two form a disulfide bond in the C-terminal domain.
source: Of the seven cysteines in the ER-lumenal portion of TAPBPR, four are involved in two disulfide bridges in the N-terminal domain, and two form a disulfide bond in the C-terminal domain (Jiang et al., 2017; Thomas and Tampé, 2017; Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous structural studies and Figure 4A.

claim: The seventh cysteine residue, C97, is surface-exposed and located opposite to the concave surface in the N-terminal domain.
source: The seventh cysteine residue, C97, is surface-exposed and located opposite to the concave surface in the N-terminal domain (Thomas and Tampé, 2017; Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous structural studies and Figure 4A.

claim: Mutating C97 to alanine was shown to have no effect on the catalytic activity of TAPBPR.
source: Mutating C97 to alanine was shown to have no effect on the catalytic activity of TAPBPR (Neerincx et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: C97 is not engaged in an intermolecular disulfide bond with UGGT1.
source: With respect to UGGT1 binding, C97 is not engaged in an intermolecular disulfide bond with UGGT1, but seems necessary for the interaction with UGGT1 in immunoprecipitates (Neerincx et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: C97 seems necessary for the interaction with UGGT1 in immunoprecipitates.
source: With respect to UGGT1 binding, C97 is not engaged in an intermolecular disulfide bond with UGGT1, but seems necessary for the interaction with UGGT1 in immunoprecipitates (Neerincx et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: HeLaM cells expressing TAPBPRC97A instead of TAPBPRwt displayed an altered peptide repertoire with a decrease in canonical anchor residues for HLA-A*68:02 and an increasing amount of peptide-deficient HLA-A*68:02.
source: In addition, HeLaM cells expressing TAPBPRC97A instead of TAPBPRwt displayed an altered peptide repertoire with a decrease in canonical anchor residues for HLA-A*68:02 and an increasing amount of peptide-deficient HLA-A*68:02 (Neerincx et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: UGGT1 exhibited consistently and significantly higher reglucosylation activity towards the mutant MHC I-TAPBPRC97A complex than towards the wildtype complex.
source: To our surprise, UGGT1 exhibited consistently and significantly higher reglucosylation activity towards the mutant MHC I-TAPBPRC97A complex than towards the wildtype complex (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Unless the Jun-Fos zippers have been removed, neither low- nor high-affinity peptides could bind to the tethered MHC I-TAPBPR complexes.
source: Unless the Jun-Fos zippers have been removed, neither low- nor high-affinity peptides could bind to the complexes (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), verifying that the observed differences in reglucosylation are not caused by different peptides.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The interaction between UGGT1 and HLA-A*68:02-TAPBPR was not affected by the C97A mutation.
source: Furthermore, in a pull-down experiment with UGGT1 (3 µM) using Man9GlcNAc2-HLA-A*68:02 bound to Twin-Strep-tagged TAPBPR (5 µM) and captured on Strep-Tactin Sepharose, we observed that the interaction between UGGT1 and HLA-A*68:02-TAPBPR was not affected by the C97A mutation (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: In the eluate of the pull-down experiment, the degradation product at ~37 kDa representing the C-terminal catalytic glucosyltransferase domain of UGGT1 was not present, indicating that the interface of UGGT1 with HLA-A*68:02-TAPBPR extends beyond the glucosyltransferase domain.
source: We also noticed that in the eluate of this pull-down experiment, the degradation product at ~37 kDa representing the C-terminal catalytic glucosyltransferase domain of UGGT1 was not present, indicating that the interface of UGGT1 with HLA-A*68:02-TAPBPR extends beyond the glucosyltransferase domain (Figure 4C, asterisk).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: UGGT1 requires calcium ions for its glucosyltransferase activity.
source: UGGT1 requires calcium ions for its glucosyltransferase activity (Trombetta and Parodi, 1992).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Ca2+ is coordinated by the DxD motif in the catalytic site that is typical of most A-type glycosyltransferases.
source: Ca2+ is coordinated by the DxD motif in the catalytic site that is typical of most A-type glycosyltransferases (Lairson et al., 2008; Roversi et al., 2017; Satoh et al., 2017; Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work and Figure 4D.

claim: The interaction with the Man9GlcNAc2-MHC I-TAPBPR complex was not affected by the active-site mutation in UGGT1D1316N which disrupts the Ca2+-coordinating DxD motif.
source: The interaction with the Man9GlcNAc2-MHC I-TAPBPR complex was not affected by the active-site mutation in UGGT1D1316N which disrupts the Ca2+-coordinating DxD motif (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The binding of UGGT1 to TAPBPR-associated Man9GlcNAc2-HLA-A*68:02 is Ca2+-independent.
source: We found no difference in the amount of UGGT1 that was pulled down by HLA-A*68:02-TAPBPR between the two different conditions (Figure 4F), suggesting that the binding of UGGT1 to TAPBPR-associated Man9GlcNAc2-HLA-A*68:02 is Ca2+-independent.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: UGGT1 is a pivotal component of the multi-chaperone machinery constituting the ER quality-control network in eukaryotes.
source: UGGT1 is a pivotal component of the multi-chaperone machinery constituting the ER quality-control network in eukaryotes.
evidence: This is supported by established scientific knowledge about UGGT1 function.

claim: Deletion of the UGGT1 gene in mice is embryonically lethal.
source: The physiological significance of this enzyme is illustrated by the fact that deletion of its gene in mice is embryonically lethal (Molinari et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: UGGT1 functions as the major eukaryotic glycoprotein folding sensor and gatekeeper in the calnexin/calreticulin cycle, preventing deglucosylated, non-natively folded N-glycosylated proteins from leaving the ER.
source: UGGT1 functions as the major eukaryotic glycoprotein folding sensor and gatekeeper in the calnexin/calreticulin cycle, preventing deglucosylated, non-natively folded N-glycosylated proteins from leaving the ER (Adams et al., 2020; Caramelo and Parodi, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Under the chosen conditions, the UGGT1-catalyzed conversion of Man9GlcNAc2-MHC I to Glc1Man9GlcNAc2-MHC I reached saturation at about 80%, similar to previous observations with rat UGGT.
source: Under the chosen conditions, the UGGT1-catalyzed conversion of Man9GlcNAc2-MHC I to Glc1Man9GlcNAc2-MHC I reached saturation at about 80%, similar to previous observations with rat UGGT (Totani et al., 2005), and could not be increased by higher temperatures or higher enzyme concentrations (Figure 2D–F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D–F and citations to previous work.

claim: The UGGT1-catalyzed conversion of Man9GlcNAc2-MHC I to Glc1Man9GlcNAc2-MHC I could not be increased by higher temperatures or higher enzyme concentrations.
source: Under the chosen conditions, the UGGT1-catalyzed conversion of Man9GlcNAc2-MHC I to Glc1Man9GlcNAc2-MHC I reached saturation at about 80%, similar to previous observations with rat UGGT (Totani et al., 2005), and could not be increased by higher temperatures or higher enzyme concentrations (Figure 2D–F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D–F.

claim: When analyzing the glucosylation reaction in the absence of TAPBPR on the isolated pMHC I charged with a high-affinity, photo-cleavable peptide, no activity was observed.
source: Importantly, when analyzing the glucosylation reaction in the absence of TAPBPR on the isolated pMHC I charged with a high-affinity, photo-cleavable peptide, we observed no activity (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The quality-control sensor UGGT1 does not act on MHC I clients that are already loaded with optimal peptide cargo.
source: This is in agreement with the expectation that the quality-control sensor UGGT1 does not act on MHC I clients that are already loaded with optimal peptide cargo.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data and established knowledge about UGGT1 function.

claim: When the high-affinity peptide was converted into dissociating low-affinity fragments by UV illumination, essentially generating a peptide-deficient, 'frustrated' MHC I, there was still no reglucosylation by UGGT1 detectable.
source: Most interestingly, when we converted the high-affinity peptide into dissociating low-affinity fragments by UV illumination, essentially generating a peptide-deficient, 'frustrated' MHC I which should meet the criteria of a bona-fide UGGT1 substrate, there was still no reglucosylation by UGGT1 detectable (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Only the addition of TAPBPR could restore UGGT1-catalyzed reglucosylation of peptide-deficient MHC I.
source: Only the addition of TAPBPR could restore UGGT1-catalyzed reglucosylation (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The strict dependence of UGGT1 on TAPBPR in acting towards HLA-A*68:02 is most likely not valid for all MHC I allomorphs, since the various allomorphs differ in their reliance on TAPBPR as a peptide editor.
source: The strict dependence of UGGT1 on TAPBPR in acting towards HLA-A*68:02 is most likely not valid for all MHC I allomorphs, since the various allomorphs differ in their reliance on TAPBPR as a peptide editor.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data and established knowledge about MHC I allomorph diversity.

claim: Experimental evidence suggests that UGGT1 can operate on MHC I in a TAPBPR-independent manner.
source: Indeed, experimental evidence suggests that UGGT1 can operate on MHC I in a TAPBPR-independent manner (Neerincx et al., 2017), and it appears that UGGT1 interacts with most HC10-reactive MHC I allomorphs independent of TAPBPR, whereas the binding of W6/32-reactive MHC I allomorphs is TAPBPR-dependent (Neerincx et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: UGGT1 interacts with most HC10-reactive MHC I allomorphs independent of TAPBPR, whereas the binding of W6/32-reactive MHC I allomorphs is TAPBPR-dependent.
source: Indeed, experimental evidence suggests that UGGT1 can operate on MHC I in a TAPBPR-independent manner (Neerincx et al., 2017), and it appears that UGGT1 interacts with most HC10-reactive MHC I allomorphs independent of TAPBPR, whereas the binding of W6/32-reactive MHC I allomorphs is TAPBPR-dependent (Neerincx et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Previous studies reported a preferred glucosylation by Drosophila UGGT1 towards the human allomorph HLA-B*08:01 when loaded with suboptimal peptides.
source: Notably, previous studies reported a preferred glucosylation by Drosophila UGGT1 towards the human allomorph HLA-B*08:01 when loaded with suboptimal peptides (Wearsch et al., 2011; Zhang et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: HLA-B*08:01 displays no detectable interaction with human TAPBPR.
source: In addition, it has been demonstrated that HLA-B*08:01 displays no detectable interaction with human TAPBPR and thus, it seems likely that UGGT1 can act on some MHC I allomorphs in a TAPBPR-independent manner (Ilca et al., 2019; Sun et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: It seems likely that UGGT1 can act on some MHC I allomorphs in a TAPBPR-independent manner.
source: In addition, it has been demonstrated that HLA-B*08:01 displays no detectable interaction with human TAPBPR and thus, it seems likely that UGGT1 can act on some MHC I allomorphs in a TAPBPR-independent manner (Ilca et al., 2019; Sun et al., 2023).
evidence: This is inferred from citations to previous work.

claim: The mutation of C97 to alanine affected neither the catalyzed reglucosylation of MHC I-TAPBPRC97A nor the interaction with the glucosyltransferase.
source: While a previous study concluded that C97 is essential for the association between TAPBPR and UGGT1 (Neerincx et al., 2017), we found that the mutation of C97 to alanine affected neither the catalyzed reglucosylation of MHC I-TAPBPRC97A nor the interaction with the glucosyltransferase (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B and C.

claim: C97 is an exposed surface residue positioned opposite the concave surface in the N-terminal domain that engulfs the α2–1 region of the MHC I, relatively close to the glycosylated N86 in the MHC I (Cα-Cα distance: 23.5 Å).
source: According to one of the TAPBPR-MHC I crystal structures (Thomas and Tampé, 2017), C97 is an exposed surface residue positioned opposite the concave surface in the N-terminal domain that engulfs the α2–1 region of the MHC I, relatively close to the glycosylated N86 in the MHC I (Cα-Cα distance: 23.5 Å; Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous structural studies and Figure 4A.

claim: Ca2+ is an essential cofactor for UGGT1 to function as a catalyst of the glucosyl transfer reaction.
source: Despite Ca2+ being an essential cofactor for UGGT1 to function as a catalyst of the glucosyl transfer reaction, we reveal that the metal ion is not required for the recognition of Man9GlcNAc2-MHC I-TAPBPR as substrate.
evidence: This is supported by established scientific knowledge about UGGT1 catalysis.

claim: The metal ion Ca2+ is not required for the recognition of Man9GlcNAc2-MHC I-TAPBPR as substrate by UGGT1.
source: Despite Ca2+ being an essential cofactor for UGGT1 to function as a catalyst of the glucosyl transfer reaction, we reveal that the metal ion is not required for the recognition of Man9GlcNAc2-MHC I-TAPBPR as substrate.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing Ca2+-independent binding.

claim: Neither the mutation of the Ca2+-coordinating DxD sequence motif in UGGT1 nor the presence of the Ca2+ chelator EGTA changed the binding of the glucosyltransferase to Man9GlcNAc2-MHC I-TAPBPR.
source: Neither the mutation of the Ca2+-coordinating DxD sequence motif in UGGT1 nor the presence of the Ca2+ chelator EGTA changed the binding of the glucosyltransferase to Man9GlcNAc2-MHC I-TAPBPR (Figure 4E and F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E and F.

claim: TAPBPR tracks down and stabilizes empty or suboptimally loaded MHC I complexes.
source: Taken together, the data we present here add to our current picture of MHC I quality control inside the ER, where UGGT1 and TAPBPR emerge as team players, with TAPBPR tracking down and stabilizing empty or suboptimally loaded MHC I complexes.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data and established knowledge about TAPBPR function.

claim: For MHC I complexes that have been deglucosylated by GluII and cannot be loaded with optimal peptide due to scarcity of suitable cargo, TAPBPR acts as a mediator for UGGT1-catalyzed reglucosylation.
source: For those MHC I complexes that have been deglucosylated by GluII and cannot be loaded with optimal peptide due to scarcity of suitable cargo, TAPBPR acts as a mediator for UGGT1-catalyzed reglucosylation.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing TAPBPR-mediated reglucosylation.

claim: The TAPBPR-UGGT1 complex promotes recycling of immature MHC I to the Glc1Man9GlcNAc2-specific calnexin/calreticulin cycle and/or to the second peptide editor tapasin inside the PLC via calreticulin.
source: Thus, the TAPBPR-UGGT1 complex promotes recycling of immature MHC I to the Glc1Man9GlcNAc2-specific calnexin/calreticulin cycle and/or to the second peptide editor tapasin inside the PLC via calreticulin (Neerincx et al., 2017; Wearsch et al., 2011).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data and citations to previous work.

claim: The in-vitro reglucosylation system consists of human UGGT1 and peptide-receptive MHC I-TAPBPR complexes containing the ER-lumenal domains of TAPBPR and the MHC I allomorph HLA-A*68:02.
source: To investigate the role of TAPBPR in the UGGT1-catalyzed quality control of MHC I, we developed an in-vitro reglucosylation system consisting of human UGGT1 and peptide-receptive MHC I-TAPBPR complexes containing the ER-lumenal domains of TAPBPR and the MHC I allomorph HLA-A*68:02.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental design described in the manuscript.

claim: The conditions of the experimental system mimicked the peptide-depleted physiological environments TAPBPR is operating in.
source: The conditions of this experimental system mimicked the peptide-depleted physiological environments TAPBPR is operating in.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental design described in the manuscript.

claim: HLA-A*68:02 was expressed as a fusion between β2m and heavy chain, with a cleavable C-terminal Fos leucine zipper domain.
source: In short, HLA-A*68:02 was expressed as a fusion between β2m and heavy chain, with a cleavable C-terminal Fos leucine zipper domain (Figure 1A), whereas the TAPBPR construct contained a cleavable C-terminal Jun leucine zipper domain and a Twin-Strep-tag (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental design shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The TAPBPR construct contained a cleavable C-terminal Jun leucine zipper domain and a Twin-Strep-tag.
source: In short, HLA-A*68:02 was expressed as a fusion between β2m and heavy chain, with a cleavable C-terminal Fos leucine zipper domain (Figure 1A), whereas the TAPBPR construct contained a cleavable C-terminal Jun leucine zipper domain and a Twin-Strep-tag (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental design shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Co-expression of MHC I with TAPBPR was carried out in the presence of the alkaloid kifunensine to obtain the HLA-A*68:02 species carrying at Asn86 the Man9GlcNAc2 glycan that is recognized by UGGT1.
source: Co-expression of MHC I with TAPBPR was carried out in the presence of the alkaloid kifunensine to obtain the HLA-A*68:02 species carrying at Asn86 the Man9GlcNAc2 glycan that is recognized by UGGT1 (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental design shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The strategic approach applied in this study combines protein glycoengineering in human cells with LC-MS analysis, providing the major advantage of a fully defined glycan pattern on HLA-A*68:02 which allowed monitoring of the UGGT1-catalyzed reglucosylation in detail.
source: The strategic approach applied in this study combines protein glycoengineering in human cells with LC-MS analysis, providing the major advantage of a fully defined glycan pattern on HLA-A*68:02 which allowed us to monitor the UGGT1-catalyzed reglucosylation in detail.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental design and methodology described in the manuscript.

claim: A direct interaction between TAPBPR-MHC I and UGGT1 was demonstrated using purified human proteins.
source: We demonstrate a direct interaction between TAPBPR-MHC I and UGGT1 using purified human proteins.
evidence: This is supported by the pull-down experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: TAPBPR is both necessary and sufficient to mediate reglucosylation of the human MHC I allomorph HLA-A*68:02 by UGGT1.
source: We describe an in-vitro reglucosylation assay that is based on a combination of protein glycoengineering and top-down liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS) that enabled us to show that TAPBPR is both necessary and sufficient to mediate reglucosylation of the human MHC I allomorph HLA-A*68:02 by UGGT1.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data showing that TAPBPR is required for reglucosylation and that adding TAPBPR restores activity.

claim: TAPBPR unmediatedly aids UGGT1 in reglucosylating peptide-deficient MHC I, thereby affecting the maturation and quality control of MHC I in antigen processing and presentation beyond its peptide selector function.
source: Our findings corroborate the notion that TAPBPR unmediatedly aids UGGT1 in reglucosylating peptide-deficient MHC I, thereby affecting the maturation and quality control of MHC I in antigen processing and presentation beyond its peptide selector function.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing TAPBPR-mediated reglucosylation.
